paras: The threatened lynching of Lucinda Fowlkes took place near Keysville, Charlotte County, Virginia, in January 1881, after Fowlkes, a Black woman, was accused of killing her husband, Wilson Fowlkes, with an axe and throwing his body into a well. January dispatches said Black neighbors would have visited "summary justice" on her but for the intervention of white residents, and she was jailed for trial instead. She was convicted of first-degree murder in the Lunenburg County Court in February and hanged privately at Lunenburg Courthouse on April 22, 1881.

Wilson Fowlkes, a "colored preacher" in the first reports, had a farm on the road from Lunenburg County about two miles from Keysville, and the Richmond Dispatch said he was "held in much esteem" in both counties. By the January accounts he had grown jealous of a neighbor's attentions to his wife, whipped her severely, and told her he would shoot her if the man came onto his premises again. The neighbor was Isaac Goulding in January and Isaac Deans or Dean in April.

Early one morning in mid-January the neighbor came to the house before Fowlkes was up, and his wife, the reports said, struck her sleeping husband in the head with an axe and threw his body into the well. Word that Fowlkes had fallen into his well brought a crowd "of both colors" from Keysville, which found blood in the house and on the way to the well. She was arrested and confessed.

The killing "created much excitement among the negroes in the neighborhood," a Richmond dispatch based on a Keysville letter said, and "but for the counsels of the whites summary justice would have been visited upon the woman." The shorter Keysville wire put it that "the white people interfered to save Mrs. Foulkes from lynching." Neither version described a crowd gathering or any attack on her, or named those who threatened or protected her, and she was committed to jail for trial.

After a two-day trial in the County Court at Lunenburg, Lucinda Fowlkes was found guilty of first-degree murder about February 19 and sentenced to hang. She had no counsel until after she pleaded guilty, and no witnesses were called for her. Governor Holliday declined to interfere, and a request to commute her sentence to life imprisonment was refused.

On April 22 Sheriff J. W. Ellis led her to a scaffold inside an enclosure behind the jail at Lunenburg Courthouse, since state law required hangings to be private. Outside, a crowd of 100 by the Dispatch's count, mostly Black, took up the hymns of a preacher in her cell, and no disorder was reported. To the end she said she alone had killed her husband, that the other man was innocent, and that she did it because her husband constantly abused and beat her.

The story first ran on January 18, when the Savannah Morning News printed the Keysville wire under the headline "A Colored Preacher Murdered by His Wife," and the Louisiana Capitolian ran the same text on January 20 and again on January 22. The longer Richmond dispatch appeared the same day as "A Virginia Tragedy" in the National Republican and in papers from Lancaster to Portland, Maine. Both versions credited white residents with stopping the lynching, and the letter version identified the would-be lynchers as Black neighbors; none of the papers commented further on the threat.

Where the January wire had presented the killing as self-preservation, the Petersburg dispatch on her conviction called the murder "the most cold-blooded and atrocious ever committed in this section" and said its motive was to live with another man. The Richmond Dispatch headed its execution report "A Virginia Murderess Hanged" and called her alleged lover a "negro Lothario," and the Chicago Daily Tribune noted that no woman had been hanged in Virginia in twenty-five years. In April only a detached fragment on the Dispatch page repeated that a crowd "would have dealt summarily with the culprit but for the interference of the whites."
The first wire put the killing on Sunday morning and some versions of the Richmond letter on Saturday; the trial-based histories gave Saturday, January 15, and two April notices the 14th.
On motive, the January reports and her final statements cited her husband's threats and abuse; the trial report said she wanted to live with another man.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Lucinda Fowlkes
bases: January dispatches report that a lynching of the accused wife was threatened and prevented by white residents (A1, A3); no mob violence was carried out, and she was later tried and hanged by the state (A12, A17).

No one was killed by a crowd: the threatened 'summary justice' over the killing of her husband was averted (A1, A3), and Lucinda Fowlkes was executed under sentence of the Lunenburg County Court (A12, A17).

The killing, trial and hanging are widely and independently reported (A3, A9, A12, A17, A19), but the threatened lynching appears only in the two January versions, which likely trace to one Keysville letter (A1, A3), plus a detached fragment of uncertain attribution (A18); the detailed April histories do not mention it (A19, A21).

accounts.label: Keysville wire (Jan. 17)
accounts.gist: Beaten and threatened by a jealous husband, Mrs. Foulkes killed him to preserve her own life; white people interfered to save her from lynching and she was jailed.

accounts.label: Richmond dispatch from a Keysville letter
accounts.gist: Fearing her husband's threat to shoot her, she crushed his skull with an axe as he slept and hid the body in a well; blood led to her arrest and confession; Black neighbors were excited and only the counsels of whites prevented summary justice.

accounts.label: Trial report (Petersburg, Feb. 19)
accounts.gist: Convicted of first-degree murder; the trial showed her motive was to be rid of her husband and live with another man.

accounts.label: Execution histories
accounts.gist: Reconstructed the crime from sworn testimony and her confession; she maintained to the end that she alone did it because her husband abused and beat her, and that her alleged paramour was innocent.

framing.detail: Savannah ran the Keysville wire under 'A Colored Preacher Murdered by His Wife' in a 'Crime and Disaster' column, crediting 'the white people' with saving her from lynching.
The Richmond letter version ('A Virginia Tragedy', 'A Shocking Murder') attributed the threat to 'the negroes in the neighborhood' and its prevention to 'the counsels of the whites'.

Virginia papers treated the case as a murder, calling it 'the most cold-blooded and atrocious ever committed in this section' and heading the execution 'A Virginia Murderess Hanged', with the alleged lover a 'negro Lothario'; they did not discuss the threatened lynching.
The Chicago Daily Tribune's execution story described the crowd singing 'in their peculiar Ethiopian way' and noted no woman had been hanged in Virginia in twenty-five years.

conflicts.note: The later Virginia and Chicago histories, drawn from the trial, agree on Saturday, January 15; the Richmond State gives both 'the night of the 14th' and 'Saturday, the morning of the murder'.
The April accounts, based on sworn testimony and her own statements, agree on a form of Deans/Dean.

record_check.dossier: Only Lucinda Fowlkes was the target of the threatened lynching; Wilson Fowlkes was the victim of the homicide she was accused of.
0 killed by any crowd; the one death (Wilson Fowlkes) was a domestic homicide, and she was later hanged legally.
The would-be lynchers are described as 'the negroes in the neighborhood'; whites prevented the lynching.
Killing on Saturday, January 15, per the later trial-based accounts (Sunday in the first wire); the threat followed the discovery that day or the next.
No attempt on the jail is reported; the threat arose around her discovery and arrest, before she was committed.
Convicted of first-degree murder about February 19, 1881; governor declined to interfere; hanged at Lunenburg Courthouse April 22, 1881.
